claim: Mice were trained on an olfactory Pavlovian conditioning task with three cue types that predicted reward on 100% (CS+), 50% (CS50), or 0% (CS−) of trials.
source: We trained mice on an olfactory Pavlovian conditioning task with three cue (conditioned stimulus) types that predicted reward on 100% ('CS+'), 50% ('CS50'), or 0% ('CS−') of trials (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: Each mouse learned two odor sets (odor sets A and B), trained and imaged on separate days.
source: Each mouse learned two odor sets (odor sets A and B), trained and imaged on separate days and then, for electrophysiology experiments, presented in six alternating blocks of 51 trials during the recording sessions (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the experimental protocol.

claim: Mice developed anticipatory licking during the task.
source: Mice developed anticipatory licking (Figure 1C–D), and the rate of this licking correlated with reward probability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that subjects successfully learned the meaning of all six odors.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rate of anticipatory licking correlated with reward probability.
source: Mice developed anticipatory licking (Figure 1C–D), and the rate of this licking correlated with reward probability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that subjects successfully learned the meaning of all six odors.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subjects successfully learned the meaning of all six odors.
source: Mice developed anticipatory licking (Figure 1C–D), and the rate of this licking correlated with reward probability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that subjects successfully learned the meaning of all six odors.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between licking rate and reward probability.

claim: Neuropixels probes were used to record from 11 brain regions including five PFC subregions, olfactory cortex, motor cortex, and striatum.
source: Using Neuropixels 1.0 and 2.0 probes (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2021), we recorded the activity of individual neurons in PFC, including anterior cingulate area (ACA), frontal pole (FRP), prelimbic area (PL), infralimbic area (ILA), and orbital area (ORB) (Wang et al., 2020b; Laubach et al., 2018). We also recorded from: secondary motor cortex (MOs), including anterolateral motor cotex (ALM), which has a well-characterized role in licking Chen et al., 2017; olfactory cortex (OLF), including dorsal peduncular area (DP), dorsal taenia tecta (TTd), and anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), which receive input from the olfactory bulb (Igarashi et al., 2012; Mori and Sakano, 2021); and striatum, including caudoputamen (CP) and nucleus accumbens (ACB), which are major outputs of PFC (Heilbronner et al., 2016, Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with citations to methods papers.

claim: Longitudinal 2-photon calcium imaging was performed in PL to track individual neurons across multiple days.
source: In a separate group of mice, we performed longitudinal 2-photon calcium imaging through a Gradient Refractive Index (GRIN) lens to track the activity of individual neurons in PL across several days of behavioral training (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the imaging experiments.

claim: 5332 individual neurons were isolated across 5 mice in the electrophysiology experiment.
source: In the electrophysiology experiment, we isolated the spiking activity of 5332 individual neurons in regions of interest across 5 mice (449-1550 neurons per mouse, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with specific numbers.

claim: Neurons in all regions exhibited varying degrees of modulation in response to the six cues.
source: The activity of neurons in all regions exhibited varying degrees of modulation in response to the six cues (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 2B showing neural activity across regions.

claim: There was strong modulation on CS+ and CS50 trials that appeared to be common to both odor sets.
source: Broadly, there was strong modulation on CS+ and CS50 trials that appeared to be common to both odor sets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was heterogeneity in both the magnitude and timing of neural modulation relative to odor onset across regions.
source: Across regions, there was heterogeneity in both the magnitude and the timing of the neural modulation relative to odor onset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reduced rank kernel regression was used to quantify the relative contribution of cues, licks, and rewards to neural activity.
source: To quantify the relative contribution of cues and conditioned responding (licking) to the activity of neurons in each region, we implemented reduced rank kernel regression (Steinmetz et al., 2019), using cues, licks, and rewards to predict neurons' activity on held-out trials (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with citation to the method.

claim: Neurons encoding cues accounted for 24% of all neurons.
source: Neurons encoding cues (24% of all neurons), licks (11%), or both (16%) were most common.
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentages.

claim: Neurons encoding licks accounted for 11% of all neurons.
source: Neurons encoding cues (24% of all neurons), licks (11%), or both (16%) were most common.
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentages.

claim: Neurons encoding both cues and licks accounted for 16% of all neurons.
source: Neurons encoding cues (24% of all neurons), licks (11%), or both (16%) were most common.
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentages.

claim: Neurons with any response to reward were rare, accounting for 5% of neurons.
source: Neurons with any response to reward (independent of licking) were rare (5%) (Horst and Laubach, 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentage and citation.

claim: Cue neurons were characterized by sharp responses aligned to odor onset.
source: Cue neurons were characterized by sharp responses aligned to odor onset; in contrast, lick neurons' responses were delayed and peaked around reward delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C), consistent with the timing of licks (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Lick neurons' responses were delayed and peaked around reward delivery.
source: Cue neurons were characterized by sharp responses aligned to odor onset; in contrast, lick neurons' responses were delayed and peaked around reward delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C), consistent with the timing of licks (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: The spatial distributions of cue and lick cells were noticeably different.
source: The spatial distributions of cue and lick cells were noticeably different (Figure 2E).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 2E showing spatial distribution.

claim: The differences in cue and lick coding could be described as graded across regions.
source: The differences could be described as graded across regions, with the most lick neurons in ALM, and the most cue neurons in olfactory cortex and ORB, though each type of neuron was observed in every region (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figures 2F-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: ALM had the most lick neurons.
source: The differences could be described as graded across regions, with the most lick neurons in ALM, and the most cue neurons in olfactory cortex and ORB, though each type of neuron was observed in every region (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Olfactory cortex and ORB had the most cue neurons.
source: The differences could be described as graded across regions, with the most lick neurons in ALM, and the most cue neurons in olfactory cortex and ORB, though each type of neuron was observed in every region (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Each type of neuron (cue and lick) was observed in every region.
source: The differences could be described as graded across regions, with the most lick neurons in ALM, and the most cue neurons in olfactory cortex and ORB, though each type of neuron was observed in every region (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The ranked value model (CS+>CS50>CS−) was the most frequent best model, accounting for 14% of cue neurons.
source: We found, however, that this model was the most frequent best model, accounting for 14% of cue neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentage and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: 14% of cue neurons were best explained by the untuned model with equivalent responses to all 6 cues.
source: First, there was a large fraction best explained by the model with equivalent responses to all 6 cues, which we term untuned cells (14% of cue neurons).
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentage.

claim: 35% of cue neurons were best fit by models most similar to ranked value (value-like cells).
source: We quantified the similarity to ranked value by correlating the values assigned to each cue in each model with those assigned to the cues in the ranked value model; this approach revealed an enrichment in neurons best fit by models most similar to ranked value (35% of cue neurons, Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentage and supported by Figures 3C-D.

claim: Value cells had better single-unit decoding performance for cue identity than value-like or untuned cells.
source: For individual neurons decoding the six cue identities, performance was better using value cells than value-like or untuned cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 3G showing decoding accuracy.

claim: At the population level, value, value-like, and untuned neurons performed similarly for cue identity decoding.
source: At the population level, however, all groups of neurons performed similarly (Figure 3H).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 3H.

claim: Models trained on value cells had better predictions of held-out cue value compared to value-like and untuned cells.
source: With this approach, models trained on value cells had better predictions of held-out cue value, leading to higher decoding accuracy (CS+, CS50, or CS−), compared to value-like and untuned cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 3I showing decoding accuracy.

claim: The frequency of value cells was similar across the recorded regions.
source: Interestingly, the frequency of value cells was similar across the recorded regions (Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: There were slightly more value cells across all of PFC than in motor and olfactory cortex.
source: Overall, there were slightly more value cells across all of PFC than in motor and olfactory cortex (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Olfactory cortex cue cells were less likely to encode value than cue cells in other regions.
source: Although the olfactory cortex had the most cue cells, these were less likely to encode value than cue cells in other regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Value-like cells were less frequent in motor cortex as a fraction of all neurons.
source: Value-like cells were also widespread; they were less frequent in the motor cortex as a fraction of all neurons, but they were equivalently distributed in all regions as a fraction of cue neurons (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 4B and supplements.

claim: Value-like cells were equivalently distributed in all regions as a fraction of cue neurons.
source: Value-like cells were also widespread; they were less frequent in the motor cortex as a fraction of all neurons, but they were equivalently distributed in all regions as a fraction of cue neurons (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Cue value could be decoded from value cells in each region with similar accuracy.
source: We quantified the robustness of value coding in each region by decoding cue value using selections of value cells from each region and found similar performance across all regions (Figure 1E).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 4E (note: text says Figure 1E but likely refers to Figure 4E).

claim: 5% of cue cells were best fit by the history model that incorporated trial-by-trial value estimates.
source: Overall, 5% of cue cells, including 15% of the value cells, were best fit by the history model.
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentages.

claim: 15% of value cells were best fit by the history model.
source: Overall, 5% of cue cells, including 15% of the value cells, were best fit by the history model.
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentage.

claim: History cells were present in low numbers across all regions but with higher prevalence overall in PFC than in motor and olfactory cortex.
source: Finally, we examined the regional distribution of history cells and found low numbers across all regions, but with a higher prevalence overall in PFC than in motor and olfactory cortex (Figure 5I), lending additional support for slightly enhanced value coding in PFC.
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 5I.

claim: There was a pronounced increase in neural modulation across the first session of training.
source: Visualizing the normalized activity across the imaging plane following CS+ presentation early and late in session A1 revealed a pronounced increase in modulation across this first session (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figures 6D-E showing neural activity changes.

claim: The number of individual neurons encoding cues more than doubled from early to late A1 trials.
source: The number of individual neurons encoding cues more than doubled from early to late A1 trials (Figure 6G).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 6G.

claim: The unique variance explained by cues increased across the first session, in contrast to licks and reward.
source: The unique variance cues increased across this first session, in contrast to licks and reward (Figure 6H).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 6H showing variance explained.

claim: PFC neural activity related to cues (but not licks) rapidly emerge during initial learning of the behavioral task.
source: These data indicated that PFC neural activity related to cues (but not licks) rapidly emerge during initial learning of the behavioral task.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the data showing differential emergence of cue vs lick coding.

claim: Neurons were much more correlated with their own activity on the subsequent day than would be expected by chance.
source: In fact, neurons were much more correlated with their own activity on the subsequent day than would be expected by chance (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Session A3 model predictions outperformed shuffle controls at all time points, demonstrating preservation of a learned coding scheme.
source: Session A3 model predictions were most highly correlated with true activity during A3, but they outperformed shuffle controls at all time points, demonstrating preservation of a learned coding scheme (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The preferred coding of cue, lick, and both cell groups, as defined in session A3, was preserved in earlier days.
source: The preferred coding of each group, as defined in session A3, was preserved in earlier days (Figure 7H).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 7H showing unique variance across days.

claim: Cue and lick coding are stable properties of PFC neurons across multiple days of behavioral training.
source: Thus, cue and lick coding are stable properties of PFC neurons across multiple days of behavioral training.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the stability analyses across days.

claim: Odor set A models performed similarly well at predicting both odor set A and odor set B activity.
source: Notably, odor set A models performed similarly well at predicting both odors set A and odor set B activity (Figure 8C).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 8C showing model performance.

claim: Cue, lick, and both neurons maintained their unique variance preference across odor sets.
source: Moreover, cue, lick, and both neurons maintained their unique variance preference across odor sets (Figure 8D).
evidence: Directly stated and supported by Figure 8D.

claim: Value and value-like models were the best models for 9% and 47% of cue neurons, respectively, when odor sets were imaged on separate days.
source: Even with odor sets imaged on separate days (days 5 and 6 of training, A3 and B3), we again found that the value and value-like models were the best models for sizable fractions (9% and 47%, respectively) of cue neurons, demonstrating that value coding is conserved across stimulus sets on consecutive days (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentages and supported by Figures 8E-G.

claim: Value coding is conserved across stimulus sets on consecutive days.
source: Even with odor sets imaged on separate days (days 5 and 6 of training, A3 and B3), we again found that the value and value-like models were the best models for sizable fractions (9% and 47%, respectively) of cue neurons, demonstrating that value coding is conserved across stimulus sets on consecutive days (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the modeling results across odor sets.

claim: The ability to associate reward-predicting stimuli with adaptive behavior is frequently attributed to the prefrontal cortex.
source: The ability to associate reward-predicting stimuli with adaptive behavior is frequently attributed to the prefrontal cortex, but the stimulus-specificity, spatial distribution, and stability of prefrontal cue-reward associations are unresolved.
evidence: Statement of existing knowledge in the field from the Abstract.

claim: Neurons encoding cues or licks were most common in the olfactory and motor cortex, respectively.
source: Neurons encoding cues or licks were most common in the olfactory and motor cortex, respectively.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract.

claim: Value coding was found in all regions sampled, with some enrichment in the prefrontal cortex.
source: By quantifying the responses of cue-encoding neurons to six cues with varying probabilities of reward, we unexpectedly found value coding in all regions we sampled, with some enrichment in the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract.

claim: Prefrontal cue and lick codes were preserved across days.
source: We further found that prefrontal cue and lick codes were preserved across days.
evidence: Summary statement from the Abstract.

claim: Individual prefrontal neurons stably encode components of cue-reward learning within a larger spatial gradient of coding properties.
source: Our results demonstrate that individual prefrontal neurons stably encode components of cue-reward learning within a larger spatial gradient of coding properties.
evidence: Main conclusion stated in the Abstract.

claim: Association of environmental stimuli with rewards and the subsequent orchestration of value-guided reward-seeking behavior are crucial functions of the nervous system linked to the prefrontal cortex.
source: Association of environmental stimuli with rewards and the subsequent orchestration of value-guided reward-seeking behavior are crucial functions of the nervous system linked to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Miller and Cohen, 2001; Klein-Flügge et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations.

claim: PFC is heterogeneous, with many studies noting subregional differences in neural coding.
source: PFC is heterogeneous, with many studies noting subregional differences in both neural coding Kennerley et al., 2009; Sul et al., 2010; Hunt et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020a and functional impact on Dalley et al., 2004; Rudebeck et al., 2008; Buckley et al., 2009; Kesner and Churchwell, 2011 value-based reward seeking in primates and rodents.
evidence: Statement of existing literature with multiple citations.

claim: Functional manipulations of PFC subregions exhibiting robust value signals do not always cause a discernible impact on reward-guided behavior.
source: Furthermore, functional manipulations of PFC subregions exhibiting robust value signals do not always cause a discernible impact on reward-guided behavior (Chudasama and Robbins, 2003; St Onge and Floresco, 2010; Dalton et al., 2016; Verharen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a), encouraging investigation of differences between value signals across PFC.
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: Multiple studies have observed evolving neural representations across time in PFC, calling into question the stability of PFC signaling.
source: Within individual PFC subregions, multiple studies have observed evolving neural representations across time, calling into question the stability of PFC signaling (Hyman et al., 2012; Malagon-Vina et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: Action coding is difficult to parse from value signaling, given the high correlations between behavior and task events.
source: In particular, action coding is difficult to parse from value signaling, given the high correlations between behavior and task events (Musall et al., 2019; Zagha et al., 2022) and widespread neural coding of reward-seeking actions (Steinmetz et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of methodological challenge with citations.

claim: Without a sufficiently rich value axis, it is possible to misidentify neurons as 'value' coding even though they do not generalize to valuations in other contexts.
source: Additionally, without a sufficiently rich value axis, it is possible to misidentify neurons as 'value' coding even though they do not generalize to valuations in other contexts (Stalnaker et al., 2015; Hayden and Niv, 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement of methodological consideration with citations.

claim: ALM has a well-characterized role in licking.
source: We also recorded from: secondary motor cortex (MOs), including anterolateral motor cotex (ALM), which has a well-characterized role in licking Chen et al., 2017
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citation.

claim: DP, TTd, and AON receive input from the olfactory bulb.
source: olfactory cortex (OLF), including dorsal peduncular area (DP), dorsal taenia tecta (TTd), and anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), which receive input from the olfactory bulb (Igarashi et al., 2012; Mori and Sakano, 2021)
evidence: Statement of anatomical knowledge with citations.

claim: CP and ACB are major outputs of PFC.
source: and striatum, including caudoputamen (CP) and nucleus accumbens (ACB), which are major outputs of PFC (Heilbronner et al., 2016, Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Statement of anatomical knowledge with citation.

claim: The neural correlates of this Pavlovian conditioned behavior consist of a gradient of cue and response coding rather than segmentation of sensory and motor responses.
source: Thus, our results establish that the neural correlates of this Pavlovian conditioned behavior consist of a gradient of cue and response coding rather than segmentation of sensory and motor responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the graded distribution of cue and lick coding.

claim: Surveys of value coding in primate PFC have found individual neurons correlated with stimulus-predicted value in many subregions, with the strongest representations typically in ORB.
source: Surveys of value coding in primate PFC have found individual neurons correlated with stimulus-predicted value in many subregions, with the strongest representations typically in ORB (Roesch and Olson, 2004; Sallet et al., 2007; Kennerley et al., 2009; Hunt et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: In rodents, there is a rich literature on value signaling in ORB.
source: In rodents, there is also a rich literature on value signaling in ORB (Schoenbaum et al., 2003; van Duuren et al., 2009; Sul et al., 2010; Stalnaker et al., 2014; Namboodiri et al., 2019; Kuwabara et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a), but there have also been many reports of value-like signals in frontal cortical regions beyond ORB (Otis et al., 2017; Allen et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020a; Kondo and Matsuzaki, 2021).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: There have been many reports of value-like signals in frontal cortical regions beyond ORB in rodents.
source: In rodents, there is also a rich literature on value signaling in ORB (Schoenbaum et al., 2003; van Duuren et al., 2009; Sul et al., 2010; Stalnaker et al., 2014; Namboodiri et al., 2019; Kuwabara et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a), but there have also been many reports of value-like signals in frontal cortical regions beyond ORB (Otis et al., 2017; Allen et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020a; Kondo and Matsuzaki, 2021).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: One consequence of a widely distributed value signal is that manipulating only one subregion would be less likely to fully disrupt value representations.
source: One consequence of a widely distributed value signal is that manipulating only one subregion would be less likely to fully disrupt value representations, which is consistent with the results of studies comparing functional manipulations across PFC (Chudasama and Robbins, 2003; St Onge and Floresco, 2010; Dalton et al., 2016; Verharen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data with supporting citations.

claim: There have been multiple reports of some association-related modification of odor representations as early as the olfactory bulb.
source: There have been multiple reports of some association-related modification of odor representations as early as the olfactory bulb (Doucette et al., 2011; Li et al., 2015; Chu et al., 2016; Koldaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: AON, DP, and TTd may be a crucial first step in processing and amplifying task-related input from the olfactory bulb.
source: Considering we detected value and especially value-like coding in AON, DP, and TTd, perhaps these regions are a crucial first step in processing and amplifying task-related input from the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Speculation based on the data showing value coding in these regions.

claim: AON, DP, and TTd provide input to PFC.
source: Because they provide input to PFC (Igarashi et al., 2012; Bhattarai et al., 2022), they may be an important source of the cue coding we observed there.
evidence: Statement of anatomical knowledge with citations.

claim: Previous reports have observed drifting representations in PFC across time.
source: Previous reports have observed drifting representations in PFC across time (Hyman et al., 2012; Malagon-Vina et al., 2018), and there is compelling evidence that odor representations in piriform drift over weeks when odors are experienced infrequently (Schoonover et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: Odor representations in piriform drift over weeks when odors are experienced infrequently.
source: Previous reports have observed drifting representations in PFC across time (Hyman et al., 2012; Malagon-Vina et al., 2018), and there is compelling evidence that odor representations in piriform drift over weeks when odors are experienced infrequently (Schoonover et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citation.

claim: Coding for odor association is stable in ORB and PL.
source: On the other hand, it has been shown that coding for odor association is stable in ORB and PL, and that coding for odor identity is stable in piriform (Wang et al., 2020a), with similar findings for auditory Pavlovian cue encoding in PL (Otis et al., 2017; Grant et al., 2021) and ORB (Namboodiri et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citations.

claim: Coding for odor identity is stable in piriform.
source: On the other hand, it has been shown that coding for odor association is stable in ORB and PL, and that coding for odor identity is stable in piriform (Wang et al., 2020a), with similar findings for auditory Pavlovian cue encoding in PL (Otis et al., 2017; Grant et al., 2021) and ORB (Namboodiri et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of existing literature with citation.

claim: The consistency in cue and lick representations indicates that PL serves as a reliable source of information about cue associations and licking during reward-seeking tasks.
source: The consistency in cue and lick representations we observed indicates that PL serves as a reliable source of information about cue associations and licking during reward-seeking tasks, perhaps contrasting with other representations in PFC (Hyman et al., 2012; Malagon-Vina et al., 2018).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the stability data with citations to contrasting findings.

claim: The presence of lick, but not cue coding at the very beginning of the first session of training suggests that lick cells in PL are not specific to the task but that cue cells are specific to the learned cue-reward associations.
source: Interestingly, the presence of lick, but not cue coding at the very beginning of the first session of training suggests that lick cells in PL are not specific to the task but that cue cells are specific to the learned cue-reward associations.
evidence: Inference drawn from the temporal emergence of different coding types.

claim: Mice were water restricted and maintained at around 85% of their baseline weight.
source: Mice were water restricted for the duration of the experiments and maintained at around 85% of their baseline weight (Guo et al., 2014a).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citation.

claim: Odors were -carvone, -limonene, alpha-pinene, butanol, benzaldehyde, and geranyl acetate.
source: Odors were -carvone, -limonene, alpha-pinene, butanol, benzaldehyde, and geranyl acetate (Sigma Aldrich 124931, 218367, 147524, 281549, 418099, 173495, respectively), selected because of they are of neutral valence to naive mice (Devore et al., 2013; Saraiva et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citations.

claim: The odors were selected because they are of neutral valence to naive mice.
source: Odors were -carvone, -limonene, alpha-pinene, butanol, benzaldehyde, and geranyl acetate (Sigma Aldrich 124931, 218367, 147524, 281549, 418099, 173495, respectively), selected because of they are of neutral valence to naive mice (Devore et al., 2013; Saraiva et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citations.

claim: Recordings were made using either Neuropixels 1.0 or Neuropixels 2.0 electrode arrays.
source: During recording sessions, mice were headfixed. Recordings were made using either Neuropixels 1.0 or Neuropixels 2.0 electrode arrays (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2021), which have 384 selectable recording sites.
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citations.

claim: The resulting data were automatically spike sorted with Kilosort2.5 and Kilosort3.
source: The resulting data were automatically spike sorted with Kilosort2.5 and Kilosort3 (https://github.com/MouseLand/Kilosort; RRID:SCR_016422; Pachitariu et al., 2023), v2.5 and 3.0.
evidence: Directly stated in the Methods section with citation.
